growth_story.headline: Burundi's income per person is still 28.8 percent below its 1991 peak, after a civil war, a 2015 crisis and more than two decades of near-zero growth.
growth_story.arc: Burundi's income per person peaked in 1991, and in 2025 it was still 28.8 percent below that peak, about where it first stood in 1967. From 1990 to 1997 it fell by 3.5 percent a year, with the worst losses in 1995 (13.3 percent) and 1996 (8.1 percent), as a civil war that began in 1993 spread. Since 1998 income per person has grown by an average of 0.0 percent a year: the 2000 Arusha Accord brought relative calm, but income per person rose only 0.1 percent a year over 2006–2015. The 2015 political crisis brought a fall of 2.6 percent and the loss of donor budget support. Income per person grew 0.7 percent a year over 2016–2025 and 1.8 percent in 2025, when stronger coffee and gold exports supported growth, but fast population growth limited the gains per person, and high inflation and scarce foreign currency strained the economy.

threads.title: Civil war and its long shadow
threads.text: A civil war driven by ethnic conflict began in 1993 and ended with the 2000 Arusha Accord. Income per person fell steeply through the mid-1990s and has never regained its 1991 level.

citations.title: Country Partnership Framework for the Republic of Burundi for the Period FY19-FY23
citations.quote: Stability was temporarily gained under the 2000 Arusha Accord, which ended a civil war driven by ethnic conflicts that had begun in 1993.

threads.title: The 2015 crisis and lost aid
threads.text: A political crisis around the 2015 elections ended a decade of growth and brought a contraction, and donors suspended budget support. Grants from abroad remain far below their pre-2015 level, which leaves less foreign currency and less room in the budget.

citations.title: Country Partnership Framework for the Republic of Burundi for the Period FY19-FY23
citations.quote: The 2015 political crisis interrupted a decade of growth and development. Real GDP contracted by 3.9 percent in 2015 and 0.6 percent in 2016

citations.title: Country Partnership Framework for the Republic of Burundi for the Period FY19-FY23
citations.quote: The suspension of external budget support by donors in response to the 2015 crisis heightened the need for the Government to mobilize additional domestic revenue

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Burundi
citations.quote: external grants equaled 2.6 percent of GDP, about one-quarter of pre-2015 levels. Lower financial inflows have reduced foreign-currency availability and fiscal space.

threads.title: Scarce foreign currency, high inflation
threads.text: Large budget and external deficits, financed partly by the central bank, and low reserves fueled inflation, and fuel stayed scarce. Inflation fell sharply between 2025 and 2026, but reserves remain thin.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Burundi
citations.quote: Large fiscal and current account deficits, monetary financing, high domestic debt, and low reserves have fueled inflation, crowded out productive spending, and weakened resilience.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Burundi
citations.quote: Inflation fell from 45 percent in April 2025 to 8.6 percent in April 2026.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Burundi
citations.quote: International reserves remained low at 1.5 months of imports in June; net foreign assets were negative, and fuel shortages persisted.

threads.title: Coffee and gold exports
threads.text: Higher coffee and gold exports lifted growth in 2025. Gold output rose sharply, though mining is still a small part of the economy.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Burundi

threads.title: Subsistence farming, fast population growth
threads.text: Most workers still farm mainly to feed their own households, and productivity is low. The population grows fast, so gains in total output become small gains in income per person.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes the years before 2015 as a decade of growth, but income per person rose only 0.1 percent a year over 2006–2015. The same gap shows now: the sources report strong growth in 2025, while income per person grew 1.8 percent, because the population keeps growing fast.
